documents.title: Syllabus Guidance Fall 2026 for UNH Durham and Manchester (section 1.5 Artificial Intelligence)
documents.summary: Section 1.5 of the Provost syllabus guidance recommends that instructors state clearly whether AI is allowed and offers sample statements for banning or permitting AI. It also sets rules for faculty use of AI detectors and AI-assisted evaluation of student work, with data-protection limits.
documents.stance_why: The document sets no single rule: it "recommends that instructors be very explicit" and "encourages guidance and support ... over blanket prohibition", then supplies sample statements for a ban and for permitted use, so the decision goes to instructors and the document offers templates.

units.why: The provost "recommends that instructors be very explicit" about whether AI is allowed, so this asks instructors to state AI expectations to students; P09 fits (a recommendation, hence should).
units.anchor: recommends that instructors be very explicit with their students about whether any use

units.why: The sentence "This includes faculty use" extends the explicitness expectation to instructors' own AI use; closest type is P47 (instructors describe their own AI use).
units.anchor: This includes faculty use.
units.policy: The recommendation that instructors be explicit about AI tools includes faculty use of them.
units.fit_note: Does not say disclose to students directly; says explicitness covers faculty use.

units.why: "encourages guidance and support in students' use of generative AI over blanket prohibition" sets the university lean toward guided use rather than bans; P02 is nearest although it is not a default permission for all courses.
units.anchor: encourages guidance and support in students’ use of generative AI over blanket prohibition
units.fit_note: Encourages supported use over blanket bans but leaves each course free to prohibit (a sample prohibit statement follows).

units.why: The passage cites research that "pedagogically structured use of generative AI holds learning benefits and unstructured use can harm learning"; this is evidence about AI and learning (P55) rather than a benefit claim alone (P87).
units.anchor: pedagogically structured use of generative AI holds learning benefits
units.frag_start: Research on the prevalence of use

units.why: It says "faculty play a vital role in helping students develop the critical thinking skills needed to engage with these tools responsibly" because AI is "embedded in professional and academic environments"; this treats AI use as a professional skill to teach (P44).
units.anchor: faculty play a
units.frag_start: As generative AI tools become increasingly
units.policy: Faculty play a vital role in helping students develop the critical thinking skills needed to engage with generative AI tools responsibly, ethically, and effectively, as these tools become embedded in professional and academic environments.

units.why: Resources "for designing assignments that promote authentic learning" are "available through" a SharePoint site and the Teaching and Learning Resource Hub, which is support for faculty (P63).
units.anchor: Resources for designing assignments that promote authentic learning, intellectual

units.why: "You may also consider using this AI Assessment Scale" to disclose the course policy offers a named scale of AI use levels; P05 fits, with may as the modality.
units.anchor: consider using this AI Assessment Scale as a basis for transparently disclosing
units.frag_start: You may also consider using this
units.frag_end: about generative AI in your course.
units.policy: Instructors may use an AI Assessment Scale as a basis for transparently disclosing their AI course policy and starting conversations with students.
units.fit_note: The scale itself is linked, not described, in the text.

units.why: In the sample statement, AI use is "strictly prohibited in this course, even when properly attributed", a default ban on course work (P01).
units.anchor: is strictly prohibited in this course, even

units.why: Sample text says use of AI to complete assignments "is considered academic dishonesty" handled under existing policy, which classifies misuse as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: considered academic dishonesty (as defined by UNH’s Academic Integrity Policy)
units.frag_start: The use of generative AI tools

units.why: The sample asks students to "Complete all writing assignments using your own ideas and words"; this is about not having AI produce submitted work (P19), listed as a bulleted encouragement (should).
units.anchor: Complete all writing assignments using your own ideas and words.

units.why: Students are encouraged to "Turn on version history in Microsoft Word to demonstrate your iterative writing process", i.e. keep drafts as process evidence (P26).
units.anchor: Turn on version history in Microsoft Word to demonstrate your iterative writing process.

units.why: "Be prepared to describe your work and the process you used" asks students to be able to explain their work (P30).
units.anchor: Be prepared to describe your work and the process you used.

units.why: "Ask the course instructor if you're unsure whether a tool or method is acceptable" is the ask-first rule (P10).
units.anchor: Ask the course instructor if you

units.why: Even under the ban, "Using AI to transcribe or summarize course lectures" is prohibited unless Student Accessibility Services approves; closest is P86 (AI recording or transcription), though this is a ban with an SAS exception, not a consent rule.
units.anchor: Using AI to transcribe or summarize course lectures.
units.policy: Unless specifically approved by Student Accessibility Services, students may not use AI to transcribe or summarize course lectures.
units.fit_note: Covers summarizing as well as transcribing, and the exception is SAS approval rather than consent.

units.why: "Uploading instructor-created course materials to an AI tool" is prohibited unless SAS approves, matching P49.
units.anchor: Uploading instructor-created course materials to an AI tool for the purposes of summary
units.policy: Unless specifically approved by Student Accessibility Services, students may not upload instructor-created course materials to an AI tool for the purposes of summary generation.

units.why: The ban is justified because "important for you to engage in the process of comprehending what you read, creating content, and communicating", i.e. doing the work builds skill (P41).
units.anchor: it is important for you to engage in the process of comprehending what you read

units.why: The permit sample frames AI as "a tool, not a replacement for your own thinking and learning", so the student remains the primary thinker (P32).
units.anchor: use of generative AI as a tool, not a replacement for your own thinking

units.why: "Generative AI tools can produce inaccurate responses... expected to critically evaluate and cross-verify" requires verifying output (P31).
units.anchor: expected to critically evaluate and cross-verify information produced by AI tools

units.why: "You are responsible for the accuracy of your assignments" makes students own what they submit (P29); the verification duty is coded separately as P31.
units.anchor: You are responsible for the accuracy of your assignments

units.why: "Specific assignments may permit or require the use of generative AI tools" lets assignments decide (P04); the requirement option is a side note, so P79 is not chosen.
units.anchor: Specific assignments may permit or require the use of generative AI tools.

units.why: If tools are permitted they "should be used only in the manner specified, and with caution and proper citation"; the citation duty is P24, with the scope limit noted.
units.anchor: used only in the manner specified, and with caution and proper citation to the tool
units.frag_start: then they should be used only
units.policy: If automated writing tools are permitted for an assignment, they should be used only in the manner specified, and with caution and proper citation to the tool.
units.fit_note: Also limits use to the manner specified by the assignment.

units.why: "do not share sensitive, protected, or restricted data as this may violate privacy or intellectual property laws" is a data-protection rule (P50).
units.anchor: do not share sensitive, protected, or restricted data

units.why: "When in doubt, ask your faculty member or do not use AI tools on such data" is an ask-or-abstain rule (P10); the data rule above is P50.
units.anchor: ask your faculty member or do not use AI tools on such data.

units.why: Detection software "should not be used to make definitive judgments about academic integrity" because tools "are unreliable", so this is about not relying on detectors (P39).
units.anchor: These tools are unreliable and have been shown to be biased
units.policy: AI-detection tools are unreliable and biased against certain learners, such as non-native English speakers, and should not be used to make definitive judgments about academic integrity.

units.why: Detectors "may incorrectly flag accessibility tools" and faculty "should discuss the use of accessibility tools" with SAS-approved students in advance; accessibility is the point (P97).
units.anchor: Faculty should discuss the use of accessibility tools with students
units.policy: Faculty should discuss the use of accessibility tools with students approved by UNH SAS for their use with accommodations in advance of the class.

units.why: "Student work should not be uploaded to any third-party tool, including AI detection platforms, unless that tool has been explicitly approved" and doing so is a FERPA violation, a data-protection rule for faculty (P50).
units.anchor: Student work should not be uploaded to any third-party tool, including AI detection platforms

units.why: "faculty are required to consult the approved tools list and confirm the appropriate data tier" requires use of approved tools when reviewing student work (P92).
units.anchor: faculty are required to consult the approved tools list and confirm the appropriate data tier
units.policy: Before using any tool to review or evaluate student work, faculty are required to consult the approved tools list and confirm the appropriate data tier for that use case.

units.why: Faculty "are encouraged to review the Academic Honesty and AI Policy" for guidance on "discussing expectations with students", which concerns explaining the rules to students (P66).
units.anchor: guidance on discussing expectations with students

units.why: "Only USNH approved tools ... may be used for evaluating the content of student work" restricts AI-assisted grading to approved tools, a condition on grading (P101).
units.anchor: Only USNH approved tools (such as DeepThought and Enterprise-level CoPilot through SSO) may be used

units.why: "You must disclose your use of AI-enabled tools to students" is instructor disclosure (P47).
units.anchor: You must disclose your use of AI-enabled tools to students

units.why: Faculty must be clear "that AI will not replace your own evaluation of work": the instructor, not AI, evaluates (P46).
units.anchor: AI will not replace your own evaluation of work
units.policy: Faculty must be clear to students that AI will not replace their own evaluation of work.

units.why: "Faculty who restrict student use of AI ... are expected to model the same standards of transparency" holds faculty to their own rules; nearest is P47 (disclosure and limits on instructor use).
units.anchor: expected to model the same standards of transparency and responsible use they require
units.fit_note: A modeling expectation rather than a specific disclosure act.

units.why: "departments are encouraged to establish shared norms around faculty AI use" delegates norm-setting to departments (P85).
units.anchor: departments are encouraged to establish shared norms around faculty AI use
units.fit_note: Concerns faculty AI use rather than student rules.

units.why: Using any non-USNH tool to review student work requires "explicit approval from ET&S", a condition on AI-assisted evaluation (P101).
units.anchor: faculty are required to get explicit approval from ET&S to share student work

units.why: The sample faculty statement says the instructor "may use USNH approved artificial intelligence-enabled tools ... to assist in assessing de-identified student work", which tells students of instructor AI use (P47).
units.anchor: I may use USNH approved artificial intelligence-enabled tools

units.why: The sample says AI tools "support--but not replace--my judgment as a faculty member" and findings "will be reviewed by me", keeping a human grading decision (P46).
units.anchor: Any findings from AI tools will be reviewed by me
units.policy: AI tools are used to support but not replace the faculty member's judgment, and any findings from AI tools will be reviewed by the faculty member in the context of the assignment and course learning objectives.

units.why: Students may "request that your work be reviewed by me without AI assistance", honored "without academic penalty"; no type covers an opt-out from AI-assisted grading.
units.anchor: you have the right to request that your work be reviewed by me without AI
units.uncovered_note: Students have a right to opt out of AI-assisted review of their work and have it reviewed by the instructor alone, without penalty.

units.why: The SRRR definition of plagiarism includes "computer generated text ... as one's own", classifying it as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: including computer generated text or work outsourced to third parties

units.why: Cheating is "Use or attempted use of ... AI tools ... without authorization", so unauthorized AI use is cheating (P36).
units.anchor: AI tools, assignment/exam surrogate, or other forms of assistance without authorization

documents.title: Graduate Catalog: Academic Integrity (Guidance on Permissibility of Generative AI Use in Graduate Exams and Theses)
documents.summary: The Graduate School states that it has no universal policy on AI in graduate exams and theses and gives guidance. Programs must communicate expectations, students must disclose and get committee approval, and unapproved use is misconduct.
documents.stance_why: The text says "the Graduate School does not have a universal policy" and that "some programs may prohibit ... whereas others may allow it", so the stance is delegated to programs, although it adds disclosure and approval conditions for any use.

units.why: The Graduate School "does not have a universal policy" on AI in exams and theses and only offers guidance, leaving the rule to programs (P85).
units.anchor: Graduate School does not have a universal policy regarding the permissibility of using generative AI

units.why: "Programs should explicitly communicate to students their expectations" for AI in exams and theses, in writing at matriculation and before exams; this is the statement-of-expectations duty (P09).
units.anchor: Programs should explicitly communicate to students their expectations for whether and how generative AI
units.policy: Programs should explicitly communicate to students, in writing when they first matriculate and again before their exams and theses or dissertations, their expectations for whether and how generative AI may be used.
units.fit_note: Applies to programs and graduate exams and theses rather than course syllabi.

units.why: "Some programs may prohibit ... whereas others may allow it within prescribed and clearly communicated boundaries" lets programs choose (P85).
units.anchor: Some programs may prohibit the use of generative AI for these purposes, whereas others

units.why: Programs should "develop a regular and consistent way of establishing and communicating their expectations", including "updating relevant handbooks, orientation materials, and mentor guidelines"; a communication duty (P09) with a maintenance element.
units.anchor: programs should develop a regular and consistent way of establishing and communicating their expectations
units.fit_note: Also asks programs to keep handbooks and orientation materials updated.

units.why: "Students using generative AI tools must disclose such use, including ... what tool(s) were used, how, and when" requires tool, manner and date detail (P25).
units.anchor: must disclose such use, including an explanation of what tool(s) were used, how, and when

units.why: "All such uses must be communicated to, and authorized by, the advisor and relevant academic committee": use needs prior approval; nearest is P04 (someone else decides), with approval by committee.
units.anchor: must be communicated to, and authorized by, the advisor and relevant academic committee
units.frag_start: All such uses must be communicated
units.policy: All uses of generative AI in graduate exams, presentations, theses and dissertations must be communicated to, and authorized by, the advisor and relevant academic committee.
units.fit_note: Approval is by advisor and committee for each use, not per assignment.

units.why: "must represent the student's own scholarly work" is the own-work rule (P29), here for exams, theses and dissertations.
units.anchor: must represent the student’s own scholarly work

units.why: AI may be used for "approved and clearly acknowledged purposes ... but the intellectual contributions must be the student's own" keeps the student as the thinker (P32).
units.anchor: the intellectual contributions must be the student’s own
units.frag_start: AI tools may be used for
units.policy: AI tools may be used for approved and clearly acknowledged purposes upon receiving the necessary approval from the committee, but the intellectual contributions must be the student's own.

units.why: "Any use of AI tools must be properly cited according to disciplinary norms" is a citation duty (P24).
units.anchor: Any use of AI tools must be properly cited according to disciplinary norms.

units.why: "Unapproved use of generative AI in exams, theses, or dissertations constitutes academic misconduct", so it is classed as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: Unapproved use of generative AI in exams, theses, or dissertations constitutes academic misconduct

units.why: It is "grounds for failure of the relevant exam or thesis based on the judgement of the evaluating committee", a stated penalty (P37).
units.anchor: grounds for failure of the relevant exam or thesis

units.why: "The reporting and appeals process for all academic misconduct should follow the Academic Integrity policy" points to the formal procedure (P81).
units.anchor: The reporting and appeals process for all academic misconduct should follow the
units.policy: The reporting and appeals process for AI-related academic misconduct should follow the Academic Integrity policy in the Student Rights, Rules, and Responsibilities.

documents.title: USNH Guidelines for the Use and Procurement of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) Tools
documents.summary: System-level IT guidance on using and buying generative AI tools: protect confidential data, check output, watch for phishing and consult IT before procurement. On academic integrity it defers to each institution and encourages faculty to state permitted uses.
documents.stance_why: On teaching use it says "Refer to your institution's student and faculty handbooks" and that faculty "are encouraged to clearly communicate permitted uses", so it sets no stance on coursework and hands the decision to institutions and instructors.

units.why: The bulletin "supports the responsible exploration of these tools" while flagging security, privacy, compliance, copyright and integrity; it is an institution-level framework statement (P56).
units.anchor: USNH supports the responsible exploration of these tools

units.why: "Do not input data classified as confidential or sensitive (Tier 2 and above) into publicly available generative AI tools" is a data protection rule (P50).
units.anchor: Do not input data classified as confidential or sensitive (Tier 2 and above)

units.why: "Information shared with AI tools using default settings may not be private" explains the risk behind the data rule (P50).
units.anchor: Information shared with AI tools using default settings may not be private

units.why: "Users are accountable for any content they produce or publish that incorporates AI-generated material" makes users own their output (P29).
units.anchor: Users are accountable for any content they produce or publish that incorporates AI-generated material.

units.why: AI content "may be inaccurate, misleading, or fabricated (commonly referred to as hallucinations)" and "could contain copyrighted material"; the accuracy warning is P31 and the copyright point is added.
units.anchor: AI-generated content may be inaccurate, misleading, or fabricated
units.fit_note: Also notes AI content could contain copyrighted material.

units.why: "All AI-generated content should be carefully reviewed for accuracy and compliance before dissemination" asks users to verify output (P31).
units.anchor: All AI-generated content should be carefully reviewed for accuracy and compliance

units.why: "Refer to your institution's student and faculty handbooks for policies on academic integrity" tells users to find the applicable rules (P78).
units.anchor: Refer to your institution’s student and faculty handbooks for policies on academic integrity.
units.fit_note: Points to institutional handbooks, not each course.

units.why: "Each USNH institution or department may update its policies" allows institutions and departments to set their own rules (P85).
units.anchor: Each USNH institution or department may update its policies

units.why: "Faculty are encouraged to clearly communicate permitted uses of AI in coursework" asks instructors to state expectations (P09).
units.anchor: Faculty are encouraged to clearly communicate permitted uses of AI in coursework

units.why: "Students should proactively seek clarification from instructors when necessary" is the ask-when-unsure rule (P10).
units.anchor: Students should proactively seek clarification from instructors when necessary.

units.why: "Generative AI has enabled malicious actors to craft increasingly sophisticated phishing scams" and users should report suspicious messages; security awareness (P75).
units.anchor: report any suspicious communications to ET&S Client Services
units.policy: Users continue to follow cybersecurity best practices and report any suspicious communications to ET&S Client Services, because generative AI has enabled more sophisticated phishing scams.

units.why: Before acquiring generative AI tools, users "consult with ET&S" or request a Security Assessment Review, which is institutional review of tools (P65).
units.anchor: consult with ET&S about options

units.why: "Any vendor-provided AI tools must undergo a risk assessment by the USNH Cybersecurity team before use" is review before deployment (P65).
units.anchor: Any vendor-provided AI tools must undergo a risk assessment by the USNH Cybersecurity team

units.why: USNH "will continue to monitor advancements, gather feedback ... and update these guidelines accordingly", a commitment to revisit (P54).
units.anchor: USNH will continue to monitor advancements, gather feedback from the university community

units.why: "These guidelines build on existing USNH policies rather than introducing new requirements" ties AI use to existing policy (P77).
units.anchor: These guidelines build on existing USNH policies rather than introducing new requirements.

notes: Only university-layer documents were in the collect file; no school, computing or course documents. Syllabus guidance is a 43k-char document and only section 1.5 concerns AI; other sections (class recording, academic integrity penalties) were not AI-specific and not coded.
